Florida Medical Marijuana Patients Travel to Orlando to Denounce "Marijuana Education Summit"

FOR IMMEDIATE RELEASE

Contact Toni Leeman, President or Irvin Rosenfeld, Legal Patient
Beeper: 888-487-0252 1-800-255-1943

Marijuana Patients Travel to Orlando to Denounce "Marijuana Education Summit"

Elvy Musikka and Irvin Rosenfeld are two "legal" patients who receive medical marijuana every month from the federal government. Upon learning of the "Marijuana Education Summit" being sponsored by the Florida Department of Law Enforcement and Drug Free America Foundation, they offered to relate their personal knowledge to the audience. However, the sponsors refused to allow them to address the conference.

On May 27, 1998 Elvy Musikka, Irvin Rosenfeld and Greg Scott will directly contradict the distorted information being distributed at the conference by offering personal testimony on the benefits of marijuana as medicine. They will address the press at 12:30 P.M. in front the Adam’s Mark Hotel located at 1500 Sand Lake Road, Orlando.

"Although the brochure [about the summit] claims they will present ‘comprehensive information’ on medical marijuana, there’s no one talking about the benefits of medical marijuana," claims Irvin Rosenfeld. "I offered to debate any one of the top guns they’ve brought in from Washington, but they refuse. They’re unwilling to face the fact that marijuana is medicine."

"The State of Florida and the United States Government have said that marijuana is medicine for me. It has saved me from going blind. Why do they refuse to help the thousands of other people suffering with glaucoma and other diseases?" asked Elvy Musikka, another "legal" patient receiving 300 marijuana cigarettes per month from the government. "They say glaucoma is the leading cause of blindness in this country, I say ignorance is the leading cause."

Elvy Musikka and Irvin Rosenfeld are Florida residents and two of only eight patients in the United States who receive marijuana under the now defunct "Investigative New Drug Compassionate Access Program" which began in the 1970's. Greg Scott, another Floridian and an AIDS patient using marijuana, will offer himself as living proof that marijuana is medicine, and indeed saved his life.

In the early 1990's people suffering with AIDS applied to the Compassionate Access Program when they discovered that one of marijuana’s effects is to stimulate their appetite and helped combat AIDS wasting syndrome. They also found that smoking marijuana was easing the constant nausea associated with the medications they were taking. The program was abruptly closed under the Bush administration in response to a flood of AIDS applicants. It remains closed today, except for the eight patients originally approved.
